text: What are the primary differences between an array and a linked list in terms of memory layout and access time?
idealAnswer: Arrays allocate contiguous blocks of memory allowing O(1) random access via index arithmetic, but have fixed capacity and costly O(n) insertions. Linked lists store elements non-contiguously connected by pointers, providing dynamic sizing and O(1) insertions at known nodes, but require O(n) traversal.

conditions.name: Contiguous vs Pointer-Linked Memory Allocation
Random Access Complexity vs Traversal Overhead
Insertion and Deletion Dynamic Resizing Trade-offs

text: Explain the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) and First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principles using Stack and Queue data structures with real-world use cases.
idealAnswer: A Stack enforces LIFO semantics where the most recently pushed element is popped first, utilized in recursion call stacks, undo buffers, and syntax parsing. A Queue enforces FIFO semantics where the earliest enqueued element is dequeued first, utilized in task scheduling, message brokers, and breadth-first search.

conditions.name: LIFO Principles and Stack Operations
FIFO Principles and Queue Operations
Real-World Systems Applications

text: How does the Binary Search algorithm achieve logarithmic time complexity, and what precondition must the dataset meet?
idealAnswer: Binary search requires the dataset to be strictly sorted. At each step, it compares the target value against the median element and discards half the remaining search space, halving problem size from n to n/2 iteratively, yielding O(log n) time complexity with O(1) auxiliary space.

conditions.name: Sorted Array Precondition Requirement
Divide-and-Conquer Search Space Halving
Logarithmic O(log n) Complexity Analysis

text: What is Big-O notation, and why is it used to evaluate the efficiency of algorithms?
idealAnswer: Big-O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm asymptotic runtime or memory consumption as input size n grows towards infinity. It abstracts hardware variance, clock speed, and compiler optimizations to classify algorithms into standard complexity classes like O(1), O(n), and O(n log n).

conditions.name: Asymptotic Upper Bound Definition
Hardware Independence and Input Scaling
Standard Complexity Classes Classification

text: What is the fundamental difference between a process and a thread in modern operating systems?
idealAnswer: A process is an independent program execution context with its own private virtual address space, file descriptors, and memory protection. A thread is a lightweight execution unit inside a process that shares the parent process heap, code, and resources while retaining its own private program counter and call stack.

conditions.name: Process Memory Isolation and Address Space
Thread Shared Heap and Lightweight Scheduling
Private Stack, Program Counter, and Context Switching

text: Compare TCP and UDP protocols, explaining when an engineer should choose one over the other.
idealAnswer: TCP is a connection-oriented protocol providing guaranteed ordered delivery, packet retransmission, flow control, and error checking via a three-way handshake, suited for web pages, file transfers, and APIs. UDP is connectionless and lightweight without retransmissions, suited for real-time video streaming, gaming, and DNS where low latency outweighs packet loss.

conditions.name: TCP Reliability, Handshake, and Ordered Delivery
UDP Connectionless Low-Latency Semantics
System Use Case Justification

text: Explain the difference between HTTP and HTTPS, focusing on the role of TLS/SSL encryption.
idealAnswer: HTTP transmits plaintext data across TCP port 80, making requests vulnerable to eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. HTTPS secures communication over port 443 by encrypting the HTTP transport layer using TLS/SSL, providing end-to-end data confidentiality, integrity checks, and cryptographic server authentication via digital certificates.

conditions.name: Plaintext Vulnerability vs Port 443 TLS Encapsulation
Cryptographic Encryption, Confidentiality, and Integrity
Server Identity Authentication via PKI Certificates

text: What is the practical difference between git merge and git rebase when combining branches?
idealAnswer: Git merge creates a new non-destructive merge commit combining the history of both branches, preserving the exact chronological sequence and commit graph topology. Git rebase rewrites project history by replaying local commits on top of the target base branch, producing a clean linear history but modifying commit hashes.

conditions.name: Git Merge Non-Destructive Merge Commit
Git Rebase Linear History and Commit Replaying
Golden Rule and Public Branch Considerations

text: What are the key trade-offs between relational (SQL) and non-relational (NoSQL) database systems?
idealAnswer: Relational SQL databases use structured schemas, table relations, and ACID transactions, excelling at complex relational joins and financial integrity. NoSQL databases provide flexible schema-less models (document, key-value, column, graph) designed for horizontal scaling across distributed clusters with high write throughput and eventual consistency.

conditions.name: Structured Schema and Relational Joins in SQL
Flexible Data Models and Horizontal Scaling in NoSQL
ACID vs BASE Eventual Consistency Trade-offs

text: Explain the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) and why it improves software maintainability.
idealAnswer: The Single Responsibility Principle asserts that a class, module, or function should have only one reason to change, encapsulating a single tightly-scoped concern. Following SRP reduces class coupling, simplifies automated unit testing, avoids side-effect bugs, and ensures team members can modify modules concurrently without merge conflicts.

conditions.name: Single Reason to Change Definition
Decoupling and Side-Effect Mitigation
Maintainability and Unit Testability Benefits

text: What is recursion, and what components are required to prevent a stack overflow error?
idealAnswer: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem. Every recursive implementation strictly requires at least one terminating base case to return without recursive calls, and a recursive step that moves state toward the base case, preventing infinite recursion and call stack overflow.

conditions.name: Self-Referential Function Invocation Definition
Base Case Termination Guard
Call Stack Frame Accumulation and State Progress

text: Explain the difference between pass-by-value and pass-by-reference in modern programming languages.
idealAnswer: In pass-by-value, a copy of the actual variable data is passed to the function parameter, meaning changes inside the function do not affect the original caller variable. In pass-by-reference, the memory address or pointer reference is passed, allowing the function to directly mutate the caller original data in memory.

conditions.name: Pass-by-Value Data Copy Isolation
Pass-by-Reference Memory Pointer Mutation
Side Effects and Object Handling Behavior

text: What is a deadlock in concurrent programming, and what are the four necessary Coffman conditions required for it to occur?
idealAnswer: A deadlock is a state where concurrent threads or processes are permanently blocked because each holds a resource while waiting for another held by another thread. The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait; breaking any one condition prevents deadlocks.

conditions.name: Deadlock Definition and Resource Blocking
Four Coffman Conditions Enumeration
Deadlock Prevention and Resource Ordering Strategies

text: How do Hash Maps handle hash collisions, comparing separate chaining versus open addressing?
idealAnswer: Hash maps encounter collisions when two distinct keys hash to the same bucket index. Separate chaining stores colliding entries in linked lists or balanced red-black trees at each bucket. Open addressing resolves collisions within the table itself by probing subsequent slots using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing.

conditions.name: Hash Collision Cause and Hash Function Distribution
Separate Chaining with Lists and Balanced Trees
Open Addressing Probing Strategies and Clustering

text: Explain the internal architecture and eviction mechanics of an in-memory Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache.
idealAnswer: An efficient LRU cache achieves O(1) get and put operations by pairing a Hash Map with a Doubly Linked List. The hash map maps keys to list nodes for instant lookup, while the doubly linked list tracks access recency; on access or update, the node moves to the head, and on capacity overflow, the tail node is evicted.

conditions.name: Hash Map and Doubly Linked List Composition
Node Movement on Cache Hit and Update
Eviction Protocol on Capacity Overflow

text: Compare RESTful APIs with GraphQL, analyzing payload optimization, over-fetching, and caching capabilities.
idealAnswer: REST uses standardized HTTP verbs over resource-oriented endpoints, benefiting from ubiquitous HTTP caching, CDN edge caching, and predictable URIs, but often suffers from over-fetching and under-fetching. GraphQL exposes a single endpoint allowing clients to query exact nested fields in one roundtrip, but shifts query parsing to the server and complicates HTTP caching.

conditions.name: REST Resource Endpoints and HTTP Method Standards
GraphQL Query Flexibility Eliminating Over-fetching
Caching and Server-Side Complexity Trade-offs

text: Explain why B-Tree indexes are preferred over binary search trees for disk-based relational database storage.
idealAnswer: B-Trees are self-balancing multi-way search trees with high fan-out, meaning each node contains multiple keys and child pointers fitting exactly into disk page blocks (e.g., 4KB or 8KB). This shallow tree depth minimizes expensive disk I/O seek operations compared to deep binary search trees, and sequential leaf links facilitate fast range scans.

conditions.name: High Fan-out and Disk Page Block Alignment
Minimizing Disk I/O Seeks vs Binary Trees
Sequential Leaf Pointers for Range Scans

text: Describe the CAP Theorem and explain the practical engineering trade-offs between CP and AP distributed architectures.
idealAnswer: The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance during a network split. Because network partitions (P) are unavoidable in real networks, architectures must choose CP (refusing writes or returning errors to preserve linearizable consistency) or AP (accepting writes with eventual consistency).

conditions.name: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance Definition
Unavoidability of Network Partitions
CP Linearizability vs AP Eventual Availability Trade-off

text: What is a Race Condition in multi-threaded programming, and how do Mutexes differ from Counting Semaphores in preventing them?
idealAnswer: A race condition occurs when concurrent threads access shared mutable state without synchronization and the outcome depends on thread scheduling order. A Mutex is a binary mutual exclusion lock with ownership semantics, where only the locking thread may unlock it. A Semaphore maintains a counter representing resource permits, allowing multiple threads up to the permit limit without ownership.

conditions.name: Race Condition and Shared Mutable State
Mutex Mutual Exclusion and Ownership Semantics
Counting Semaphore Resource Permit Signaling

text: Explain the principles of Dynamic Programming, contrasting top-down memoization with bottom-up tabulation.
idealAnswer: Dynamic Programming optimizes problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by caching subproblem solutions. Top-down memoization maintains recursive structure, caching results in a hash map or array as needed on demand. Bottom-up tabulation eliminates recursion overhead by iteratively filling a DP table starting from initial base states.

conditions.name: Overlapping Subproblems and Optimal Substructure
Top-down Recursion with On-demand Caching
Bottom-up Iterative Tabulation and Space Optimization

text: How does virtual memory work, and what sequence of events occurs when a page fault happens?
idealAnswer: Virtual memory isolates process address spaces by mapping virtual addresses to physical RAM frames through page tables managed by the CPU MMU. When a process accesses an unmapped or swapped-out virtual page, the MMU triggers a page fault hardware interrupt. The OS pauses the thread, reads the requested page from disk swap into a free physical frame, updates the page table, and resumes execution.

conditions.name: Virtual Address Mapping via MMU and Page Tables
Page Fault Hardware Interrupt Detection
OS Disk Swap Retrieval and Page Table Update

text: Explain the four ACID properties of relational databases and how transaction isolation levels balance consistency against throughput.
idealAnswer: ACID guarantees Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (schema constraints preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions execute without interference), and Durability (committed changes survive crashes via write-ahead logs). Isolation levels like Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable balance anomalies like dirty reads and phantom reads against lock contention.

conditions.name: ACID Principles Definition and Guarantees
Concurrency Anomalies Characterization
Isolation Levels Spectrum from Read Committed to Serializable

text: Contrast Depth-First Search (DFS) and Breadth-First Search (BFS) in graph traversal, including data structures and optimal use cases.
idealAnswer: DFS traverses deeply along branches before backtracking using a Stack or recursion, requiring O(V) space proportional to search depth, ideal for topological sorting, cycle detection, and maze generation. BFS explores neighbor nodes layer-by-layer using a Queue, requiring O(V) space proportional to maximum width, guaranteeing shortest path in unweighted graphs.

conditions.name: DFS Stack Mechanism and Deep Branch Backtracking
BFS Queue Mechanism and Level-by-Level Exploration
Shortest Path and Topological Sorting Use Cases

text: How do you detect cycles in directed versus undirected graphs, and how does Kahn algorithm implement topological sorting?
idealAnswer: Undirected graph cycles are detected via DFS by tracking visited nodes and checking for edges to visited non-parent nodes, or via Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find). Directed graphs require tracking the active recursion stack in DFS (three-color marking: unvisited, visiting, visited). Kahn algorithm computes in-degrees for all nodes, enqueues 0-in-degree nodes iteratively, detecting cycles if output length is less than total vertices.

conditions.name: Cycle Detection in Directed Graphs with Recursion Stack
Undirected Graph Cycle Detection via Parent Tracking or DSU
Kahn Algorithm In-Degree Processing for Topological Sort

text: Explain how the Raft consensus algorithm guarantees safety, leader election, and log replication across a distributed cluster.
idealAnswer: Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and commitment safety. Nodes start as followers and transition to candidates upon randomized election timeouts, requesting votes from peers with majority approval required. The elected leader appends incoming client entries to its log and sends AppendEntries RPCs to followers; once replicated on a quorum majority, the entry commits, ensuring State Machine Safety across server crashes.

Log Replication and Quorum AppendEntries Protocol
State Machine Safety and Log Consistency Guarantees

text: Compare the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol with the Saga pattern for distributed transactions in microservices architectures.
idealAnswer: Two-Phase Commit enforces synchronous atomic consistency across distributed databases using a coordinator that sends Prepare and Commit/Abort phases, but suffers from blocking coordinator failure and high latency. The Saga pattern decomposes transactions into a series of asynchronous local transactions coordinated via choreography or orchestration, utilizing compensating transactions to undo actions on failure, prioritizing availability over immediate consistency.

conditions.name: Two-Phase Commit Synchronous Prepare and Commit Phases
Saga Pattern Choreography, Orchestration, and Compensation
Availability, Latency, and Eventual Consistency Trade-offs

text: How do Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) and Vector Clocks enable decentralized conflict resolution without central locks?
idealAnswer: Vector clocks track causal ordering in distributed systems by maintaining a vector of logical timestamps across nodes, allowing detection of concurrent concurrent updates versus causally dependent events. CRDTs provide mathematically convergent data structures (state-based CvRDT with monotonic join semilattices, or operation-based CmRDT with commutative operations) that guarantee identical state on all replicas once all updates are delivered without central locks.

conditions.name: Vector Clocks and Causality Tracking Mechanics

Decentralized Peer-to-Peer Replication Guarantees

text: Design a distributed rate limiter supporting millions of requests per second, comparing Token Bucket against Sliding Window Counter algorithms.
idealAnswer: A high-throughput distributed rate limiter uses a Token Bucket algorithm allowing configurable burst capacity refilled at a constant rate, or a Sliding Window Counter combining current and previous sub-window counts for memory-efficient smoothed limits. To achieve low latency and horizontal scale, rate state is stored in Redis clusters using atomic Lua scripts or local memory caches with async batch synchronization to avoid central network bottlenecks.

conditions.name: Token Bucket vs Sliding Window Counter Mechanics
Distributed Storage with Redis Clusters and Atomic Lua Scripts
High-Throughput Caching and Asynchronous Batching

text: Explain zero-copy I/O techniques, comparing standard read/write syscalls with sendfile, mmap, and Linux epoll for high-concurrency servers.
idealAnswer: Standard read/write syscalls incur multiple CPU data copies between disk, kernel page cache, and user space buffers, plus costly user/kernel context switches. Zero-copy techniques like sendfile and splice transfer data directly between kernel buffers and network sockets without user-space duplication. Paired with Linux epoll O(1) event-driven notification, high-concurrency servers handle tens of thousands of connections with minimal CPU overhead.

conditions.name: Kernel Buffer Copies and Context Switch Overhead
sendfile, mmap, and Direct Socket Streaming Protocols
Linux epoll O(1) Event-Driven Concurrency Scaling

text: How do you design high-scale caching architectures to prevent Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd) and Cache Penetration?
idealAnswer: Cache stampede occurs when a high-traffic key expires, causing hundreds of concurrent requests to hit the database simultaneously; it is mitigated using distributed mutex locking (e.g. Redis Redlock), probabilistic early expiration (XFetch algorithm), or background asynchronous cache refreshing. Cache penetration by non-existent keys is solved using Bloom Filters in front of the cache and caching null values with short TTLs.

conditions.name: Cache Stampede / Thundering Herd Root Cause and Mutex Locks
Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch) and Async Warmup
Cache Penetration Defense via Bloom Filters and Null Caching
